title: MB8-06453
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants are a father and son. The principal claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Nigeria, while his son XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of Ecuador. They are both claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The principal claimant acted as designated representative for his minor son. Consideration of parental consent regarding associate claimant's mother

A parental authorization in the form of a notarized declaration1 dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 from the associate claimant's mother was deposited by the claimants at the hearing. The Panel notes that the document is fulsome in terms of granting her son permission to accompany his father to Canada for the purpose of remaining with him to pursue, 'visas, refuge et nationalité.'2

Moreover, other documentation3 in the file established that the associate claimant's mother had traveled with the claimants to the United States where she had lived with them, while the three pursued asylum claims. Consequently the Panel found, on a balance of probabilities that the principal claimant had had the permission of his son's mother when the two arrived in Canada to seek refugee protection.
The claimant belongs to the Yoruba ethnic group, a Muslim by birth, and was born and raised in Lagos State.
The principal claimant's father is a XXXX XXXX of the 'Amadiyat Muslim Organization' in Nigeria.
In 1992, the principal claimant converted to Christianity and his family was furious.
He was insulted and threatened and his father warned him of the danger that could occur.
In 1994, the principal claimant's father's home was burned to the ground by a Muslim cleric and his supporters. The principal claimant himself was injured, believing that he was the intended target.
Prior to leaving Nigeria later the same year, the principal claimant was homeless and continued to receive threats. His uncle helped him to leave the country by providing money.
During the following years, the principal claimant lived in the Ivory Coast and Guinea Bissau.
He subsequently travelled to Ecuador where he XXXX XXXX and met his common-law wife and shortly before leaving the country, the minor claimant was born.

While in Ecuador the principal claimant was abducted and injured by unknown men and was not provided with help when he went to the police who insulted him as being 'illegal'. He added that his wife had been attacked several times, and some family members were killed.
The principal claimant and his spouse and the minor claimant then travelled through South and Central America to the USA where they asked for asylum in 2013.
Before the claims were finalized, the principal claimant's spouse was deported.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, the claimants crossed into Canada using an unguarded road and asked for refugee protection.
The principal claimant fears that were he to return to Nigeria, the members of his father's Muslim organization would seek to kill him for his conversion to Christianity.

The minor claimant's Basis of Claim form4 contained no allegations whatsoever, nor was a country provided against which he sought refugee protection. At the outset of the hearing, the Panel sought clarification from the principal claimant's counsel and was advised that the minor claimant was seeking refugee protection against Ecuador based on his father's allegations. While unclear what link the minor claimant made with his father whose claim was against Nigeria, during the hearing the principal claimant testified that his son's claim was based on treatment due to his race as we was seen to be an 'African' like his father.
The Panel finds that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection". The reasons are provided below.
The Panel found that the principal claimant had a viable Internal Flight Alternative in the cities of Lagos and Benin City.

The Panel found that the minor claimant failed to establish his allegations, having found the principal claimant's testimony with respect to Ecuador upon which his own claim was based to lack credibility, and that in a prospective lens, he did not establish that he would face a serious possibility of persecution based on his race. ANALYSIS Identity

The identity of the principal claimant as a national of Nigeria was established, on a balance of probabilities by an attested original birth registration and secondary documents issued during his residency in the USA, repeating the same name and date of birth5.
The identity of the minor claimant was established by supporting documentation filed into evidence, which includes a copy of his seized Ecuadorian passport.6 Nexus

With regard to the allegations of the principal claimant, the Panel finds that a nexus exists as his conversion to Christianity engages the Convention ground of religion. His claim will therefore be analyzed under section 96 of the IRPA.

With regard to the allegations of the minor claimant, the Panel finds that a nexus exists as his origins engage the Convention ground of race. His claim will therefore be analyzed under section 96 of the IRPA. Principal Claimant: IFA
The Panel found that the determinative issue with regard to the principal claimant's claim was the existence of an Internal Flight Alternative in Lagos and Benin City.

In arriving at its conclusion, the Panel accepted that the principal claimant had changed his religion and had been targeted in Lagos State. The Panel emphasizes that the principal claimant based the claim on his fear of non-state actors, namely a Muslim organization composed of clerics and members. While he briefly testified as to a fear of the police, the principal claimant explicitly testified that it was based on their having failed to provide him protection, making no link whatsoever to the principal agents of persecution, either directly or indirectly.

The Panel is guided by the Jurisprudential Guide in TB7-19851 addressing internal flight alternatives in major cities in south and central Nigeria for claimants fleeing non-state actors. The Panel finds that the principal claimant does have a viable internal flight alternative in Lagos and Benin City. There is no serious possibility of persecution in Lagos or Benin City Prong I: Security

The principal claimant fears the Amadiyat Muslim Organization. When asked by the Panel if he could relocate to Lagos or Benin City, he replied that the organization was everywhere in Nigeria. As to how the organization would be able to find out that he had returned, in order to locate him, the principal claimant replied, 'if one person sees you, they will start telling each other.' When asked if there would be another means of locating him, the he did not answer the question, stating that, 'the trauma on my body, I will never be safe'. He added that his lack of safety was due to his conversion, as he would continue to practice his religion. This aspect will be analyzed under Prong II - reasonableness.

With regard to Benin City, the principal claimant added that people who come from abroad would get kidnapped, adding that there were also Muslims there and he would be scared to walk on the street. As to how the same agents would have the capacity to locate him there, the principal claimant testified that he was not sure that they could locate him, adding, 'one person will notice you and then other people know.'

As to whether he had any proof that the individuals he feared were still active, the principal claimant told the Panel that they are aware and the organization is still alive. He added that his father had been killed by the organization, as a result of mental disturbance. With regard to this last comment, the Panel noted that the principal claimant had not linked his father's death due to the organization in his narrative, and asked for an explanation. The principal claimant explained that his conversion had led to his father's death, and it made him feel very bad.

The Panel finds the linkage of his father's death (in 2008 according to question 5 in his Basis of Claim form7), with his own conversion over fifteen years earlier to be lacking in credibility. The Panel would reasonably expect the principal claimant to set out his father's subsequent treatment by the organization leading to his death. His sadness does not excuse an omission of this importance. The omission is material and the Panel therefore rejects that his father's demise can form part of the reasons that the principal claimant would be unsafe in Lagos or Benin City.

The Panel finds that the principal claimant failed to demonstrate how he would be located beyond being randomly recognized in cities with millions of inhabitants, over twenty-four years after he had left the country. He failed to provide any specific evidence to support that he could not live in these cities and would be personally targeted there. The Panel finds that the principal claimant has failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that he would be located by the agents of persecution in Lagos or Benin City. Therefore the Panel finds that the principal claimant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in either of the proposed IFA cities.

The principal claimant also testified that he could not live securely in Benin City because he risked being kidnapped there. However, he did not explain how he would be susceptible to kidnapping more than the rest of the general population. He did not back up his statement with specific evidence. The Panel is unable to find specific evidence pointing to a greater risk for returnees to face kidnapping in either of the proposed IFAs. Consequently, the Panel finds that the risk is generalized such that the claimant has failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that he would be subjected personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, in either of the of the proposed IFA cities. Prong 2: Reasonableness Reasonable to expect the claimant to relocate.

The Panel asked the principal claimant to imagine if he were back in Lagos or Benin City, and asked what would happen. He addressed work and religion as the obstacles to resettlement. The Panel will nevertheless consider the criteria set out in the jurisprudential guide. Transportation, Travel and language

The Panel adopts the reasoning of paragraphs 23-24 and 41-42 of TB7-19851 and finds that both Lagos and Benin City are viable IFAs in terms of transportation, travel and language. Both cities have international airports, so no undue hardship exists.

The principal claimant speaks English and Yoruba, both of which are widely spoken in Lagos and Benin City. No evidence was presented to the Panel that language would be an obstacle. Consequently, these criteria would not render IFAs unreasonable in either city. Education and employment

The principal claimant testified that there was no work in Nigeria and that he, 'could not survive there.' He added that there was no work if one was not a professional. However, as to work experience, the principal claimant stated that he worked as a XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX. He nevertheless testified that without a big boss, which the Panel understood to mean connections, one could not find work. The Panel notes that the principal claimant has a high school diploma, lived in the Ivory Coast for over a decade and worked as a XXXX XXXX and has also worked as a XXXX in Ecuador as well as having had menial jobs in the USA. He indicates in his Basis of Claim form that he speaks English, Yoruba, French and Spanish. The Panel finds that principal claimant's level of education, his multi-lingual skills, combined with his work experience after two decades abroad in various countries and cultures weigh in favour of him being able to find employment, and thus conditions in the proposed IFAs would not rise to a level making it objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh in his circumstances. Ethnicity and Religion

The principal claimant in this case, like the claimant in the jurisprudential guide, is a Christian and a Yoruba. The principal claimant testified that his particular profile as a convert would bring him into conflict with Muslims. However, the Panel brought to his attention, documentary evidence8 describing the tolerance of converts by Christian and Muslim communities in Yorubaland. While not touching upon Benin City specifically, the Panel finds for the same reason as in the jurisprudential guide9, the factors of religion and indigeneship would not rise to the level necessary to make the proposed IFA unduly harsh in either of the proposed IFA cities. Availability of medical and mental health care

The Panel adopts the reasoning of paragraph 29 of TB7-19851 and finds that both Lagos and Benin City are viable IFAs in terms of the availability of medical and mental health care. Hypothesis of return with the minor claimant

The principal claimant's son has no status in Nigeria. The Panel finds that it is premature to undertake an analysis incorporating the minor claimant into the analysis under IFA. A parental authorization10 was deposited by the associate claimant's mother permitting the minor claimant to remain with his father in Canada for immigration purposes. However, despite the principal claimant's serious concerns about his son's ability to survive there, the Panel finds that the prospect of his son accompanying him back to Nigeria is purely speculative.

It is the principal claimant's burden to show that either of the two prongs of the IFA test have not been met. The Panel finds that the principal claimant has failed to discharge his burden. As the Panel finds that the principal claimant has a viable IFA in Lagos or in Benin City, he has failed to establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution in all parts of Nigeria, or that he would be subjected personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. Consequently, the principal claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a person in need of protection. Claim of minor claimant
The Panel undertook to analyze the claim of the minor claimant were he to return to Ecuador. The Panel notes that he was an infant when he left Ecuador in XXXX and is a XXXX XXXXyear-old boy.

As the principal claimant stated that the minor son based his claim on his own experiences in Ecuador that he set out in his narrative, the Panel analyzed the elements raised in his narrative when he himself was living there.
In this regard, the Panel finds that the principal claimant was not a credible witness. Omission as to role of family of minor claimant's mother

The principal claimant testified that his spouse's family rejected her because of the principal claimant's origins. He further added that he had had major problems with his spouse's brothers. He testified that he was attacked twice, the first time being when he received a serious head injury and realized later that the brothers were the attackers, while he explained that the second time, one of the two brothers, a member of the military had abducted him, and threatened him that if he did not leave his sister he would be killed. He added that not only did he fear this brother, but he feared his friends in the military as well. A parallel omission noted by the Panel was the rejection by the family of the minor claimant as a result of his father's racial heritage, and the ostracism that his spouse had also experienced from her family. It is to be noted that while the principal claimant wrote that his spouse had been attacked herself as well, he did not provide any coherent context or details. The Panel brought to the principal claimant's attention that the profile of the minor son's uncles and their roles in the treatment he and his spouse allegedly underwent had been omitted and sought an explanation. The principal claimant stated that he did not know that he had to provide separate information with regard to his son. He added that he did not want to mention his spouse's brother and the military gang.

The Panel rejects these explanations. The Panel notes that the principal claimant wrote in detail about his experiences in Ecuador. He specifically mentioned his spouse as well as what happened to him while living in the country, making reference to the first attack which he described as the work of unknown individuals. In this context, the Panel would reasonably expect the principal claimant to make the clear link to his spouse's siblings. The omission is material. Furthermore, the Panel was represented by experienced counsel whose name appears on the Basis of Claim form as the counsel of record, as well as the Basis of Claim form of the minor claimant. The Panel finds that these important omissions undermine the principal claimant's credibility, and to the extent that this omitted profile is presented as a basis to analyze the minor claimant, his credibility as well. Anomaly regarding whereabouts of minor claimant's mother

The principal claimant testified that after being deported from the USA, his spouse remained in Mexico because she remained fearful about returning to Ecuador. The Panel asked him if she had been back to Ecuador. He stated that she was in Mexico. However, the Panel brought to the principal claimant's attention that the parental authorization11 submitted in the form of a sworn declaration prepared by a Notary and signed by her in Quito on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 stated that she was a resident and domiciled in Ecuador. The principal claimant explained that he understood that his spouse had travelled to Mexico. He added that life is difficult and that they don't really communicate, and that she said that she was going to remain in Mexico.

The Panel rejects these explanations. The Panel finds that there is a clear contradiction with the principal claimant's testimony and a document that he himself provided, which at the very least situates the minor claimant's mother in Ecuador a few weeks before the hearing. The Panel finds that the contradiction was not explained. While the precise circumstances of the minor's claimant's mother's presence in Ecuador is not clear, it diminishes the credibility of the allegation of a prospective fear or risk in his country of citizenship.

The Panel acknowledges that the documentary evidence12 points to discrimination for Afro-Ecuadorans, which constitutes approximately seven percent of the population. The evidence relates to the indigenous population as well. The Panel notes that the documentation is limited and is not directed specifically to the profile of the minor claimant.

The Panel finds that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the minor claimant would, in a prospective lens meet the threshold of establishing that the discrimination he could face would be tantamount to persecution.

Given the lack of credibility of the prospective fear alleged and the insufficient objective evidence to establish it, having analyzed the evidence as a whole, the Panel finds that the minor claimant has failed to discharge his burden to establish that there is a "serious possibility" that he would be persecuted on a Convention ground. He also failed to provide any evidence that could establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should he return to Ecuador.

For all of these reasons, the Panel determines that the claimants XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees", or "persons in need of protection" and rejects their claims for refugee protection.
